content: 1. When a decision is made to treat a woman, whether she is from the general population or living with HIV, it is considered good practice to initiate treatment as soon as possible, ideally within six months. This approach minimizes the risk of losing the patient to follow-up. 2. For pregnant women, it is recommended to defer treatment until after the pregnancy has concluded, as this is considered good practice. 3. If treatment is not initiated within the six-month timeframe, it is advisable to re-evaluate the patient before proceeding with treatment. 4. The World Health Organization (WHO) suggests using large-loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) or cold knife conization (CKC) for women, whether from the general population or living with HIV, who have histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS). 5. Loop excision (LLETZ) may be preferred for women of reproductive age, in settings where LLETZ is more readily available, and when performed by providers with greater expertise in this technique. 6. Cold knife conization (CKC) may be preferred in cases where precise interpretation of the histological specimen margins is critical. 7. Evidence from a systematic review of the literature, albeit of low certainty, suggests that there may be little to no difference in the recurrence rate of AIS between CKC and electrosurgical excision. Similarly, there appears to be no significant difference in the incidence of complications such as major infections or bleeding. 8. However, the review found that women who undergo CKC may have a higher likelihood of experiencing premature deliveries in subsequent pregnancies compared to those who undergo electrosurgical excision. 9. The studies included in the systematic review did not confirm the HIV status of participants. However, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) agreed that the findings could be extrapolated to women living with HIV and applied directly to this population. 10. CKC is typically performed in an operating theatre, which may limit its accessibility in certain settings. It is also more costly and less preferred by women compared to LLETZ. 11. Additionally, greater expertise may be required to successfully perform electrosurgical excision.
